title: Say it, then stand firm
hookLine: say, I believe in Allah, and then be upright (Nawawi 21, Sufyan ibn Abdullah)
tomorrow: a man swears he'll do the basics and not one thing more. and then?
last: GOOD, OR SILENT · DON'T BE ANGRY · EVEN THE BLADE

cards: A man wants one sentence he'll never need to ask about again. Some people want the full manual; others want one line to tape to the fridge. Neither is wrong.
In al-Nawawi's twenty-first hadith, Sufyan ibn Abdullah asks for the fridge kind: tell me something about Islam I won't need to ask anyone else about. Sufyan isn't asking for a lecture.
He wants a sentence he can carry out the door, the kind you could say in a single breath. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gives him one, in two moves.

teach.b: From Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase: say, I believe in Allah, and then be upright.
The Arabic for that last part is istaqim: stand straight, stay on course, don't drift. Two moves. First you say it.
Then you stand, and standing takes the rest of your life. The Qur'an praises those who say, our Lord is Allah, and then stay upright on it, and says the angels come down to them with comfort.

teach.h: SAYING IS A DAY. STANDING IS AFTER.
teach.b: Saying is a day; standing is every day after. And notice what Sufyan asked for: something he'd never need to ask anyone else about. The answer isn't a secret fact.
It's a direction. Once you have it, the question changes from what do I believe to am I still standing in it today.
Now look back, because this was a week of standing. The tongue held at good or silent. The heat lowered before it spoke.
The blade sharpened when nobody would check. The bad deed followed by a good one. Allah kept in mind while the pages felt unfinished.
And shame left on guard. Six small ways of staying upright. None of them dramatic.
All of them standing. Next week, more of the forty.

how: Muslims often cite this hadith for steadiness over bursts; teachers pair it with Qur'an 41:30 and encourage small deeds kept up rather than big ones dropped.

o: a call to speak your mind in public
the first move: saying I believe in Allah
a phrase used only when someone converts

games.q: one sentence, two moves — tap the pairs.

s: the hadith hands over a long creed to memorize
one sentence: say, I believe in Allah, then be upright.
istaqim means stand straight and stay on course
the second move, and the longer one.
once you've said it, the hadith's work is done
saying is the first move; standing is the second, and it lasts.

games.q: you started journaling with a bang: three pages on day one. by day four, nothing. by today's hadith, what's the move?
o: go back to a small, steady amount you can keep standing on.
wait for day one's motivation to come back before writing.
start over bigger next month, with a brand-new notebook.
games.why: istaqim is staying on course after the first push: steady, not bigger.

practice: Choose one practice from this week, the one you most want to still be doing next Friday. Name the moment it's most likely to slip.
Then make the plan in one short sentence, when this happens, I'll do that, small enough to keep on your worst day, and hold it for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Say it: the hadith's first move, I believe in Allah. Then comes istaqim, the standing that takes longer, and that you keep on doing.

orig.note: Arabic: be upright, stand straight; the second move of the sentence.

carryVoice: To keep: believe, then stand, because the sentence is short and the standing is long. A week of the forty, done.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 21; Sahih Muslim 38 (Sufyan ibn Abdullah al-Thaqafi)
Qur'an 41:30, 46:13 (those who say 'our Lord is Allah' and then stay upright)
